title: Ancient endemism in a global biodiversity hotspot: an integrative revision of Tyrannochthoniini pseudoscorpions (Pseudoscorpiones: Chthoniidae) from the Western Ghats of India
content:
Abstract
The Western Ghats of India constitute one of the world’s most significant biodiversity hotspots, yet remain poorly documented for many invertebrate taxa, particularly short-range endemic leaf-litter arthropods. The pseudoscorpion tribe Tyrannochthoniini (Pseudoscorpiones: Chthoniidae), currently represented in India by only six nominal species, is revised here using an integrative systematic framework combining multilocus phylogenetic analyses (COI, H3, and 28S rRNA), species-delimitation approaches, detailed morphological examinations, and multivariate morphometric analyses. Specimens from the Western Ghats resolve into two deeply divergent, monophyletic lineages: one largely confined to the southern Western Ghats and the other to the central Western Ghats. These lineages exhibit substantial genetic divergence, a Late Jurassic origin, and statistically distinct morphospaces. Based on concordant molecular, morphological, and morphometric evidence, we propose two new genera, Sahyadrachthonius gen. nov. and Gondwanachthonius gen. nov., and describe fourteen new species (Gondwanachthonius erachiparaensis sp. nov., Gondwanachthonius edalaparaensis sp. nov., Gondwanachthonius kaikattyensis sp. nov., Gondwanachthonius urakuzhyensis sp. nov., Gondwanachthonius aralamensis sp. nov., Gondwanachthonius lambrockensis sp. nov.; Sahyadrachthonius cotigaoensis sp. nov., Sahyadrachthonius chloeae sp. nov., Sahyadrachthonius illithoduensis sp. nov., Sahyadrachthonius jibini sp. nov., Sahyadrachthonius johnsoni sp. nov., Sahyadrachthonius madikeriensis sp. nov., Sahyadrachthonius pettimudiensis sp. nov., Sahyadrachthonius selinae sp. nov.). This study establishes a robust phylogenetic framework for Tyrannochthoniini in the Western Ghats and represents the first comprehensive taxonomic revision of Indian pseudoscorpions in nearly five decades. Our findings reveal substantial previously undocumented diversity and endemism, underscoring the critical conservation importance of leaf-litter ecosystems within this global biodiversity hotspot. Conservation prioritization and sampling are essential to understand evolutionary processes and protect these microendemic lineages.
